text: Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is an increasingly common cause of chronic liver disease; however, no specific pharmacologic therapy has been shown to be effective in its treatment. The present study was designed to develop an experimental cell culture model of NASH using four kinds of fatty acids - palmitic acid (PA), stearic acid (SA), linoleic acid (LA), and oleic acid (OA) - and TNF-a, according to the two-hit hypothesis. The saturated fatty acids PA and SA are more cytotoxic than the unsaturated fatty acids OA and LA. Cellular lipid accumulation without cytotoxicity was more easily induced with the unsaturated fatty acids than with the saturated fatty acids. PA augmented TNF-a-induced cytotoxicity, while the unsaturated fatty acids attenuated TNF-a-induced cytotoxicity. In a mechanistic study, PA enhanced TNF-a-mediated apoptosis in the absence of oxidative stress, as determined by measuring the cellular glutathione and malondialdehyde levels. Moreover, PA inhibited the TNF-a-induced phosphorylation of AKT, but not c-Jun N-terminal kinase, indicating that inhibition of survival signaling pathways activated by TNF-a may explain the effects of PA on TNF-a-induced cytotoxicity. The in vitro NASH model established in this study may be used to screen drug candidates for suitability for the treatment of NASH.

EA.hy926 cells were cultured in vitro and randomly divided into control group, palmitic acid-induced insulin resistance group, total flavonoids of tartary buckwheat group and metformin group. text: /SRP:/ Immediate first aid: Ensure that adequate decontamination has been carried out. If patient is not breathing, start artificial respiration, preferably with a demand-valve resuscitator, bag-valve-mask device, or pocket mask, as trained. Perform CPR as necessary. text: /BIRDS and MAMMALS/ Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) belongs to a group of chemicals called perfluoroalkyl acids that have been extensively used in various applications such as stain and oil resistant treatments for fabrics, fire-fighting foams, and insecticides. These chemicals present an environmental and health risk being present in many samples both in wildlife and humans. In this study, we investigate the effect of PFOS on fatty acid beta-oxidation in developing chicken embryos. Fertilized chicken eggs were exposed in ovo to PFOS at day 4 of incubation. On day 10, the eggs were dissected and livers were incubated in vitro with (3)H-palmitic acid for 2 hr. The media were collected, and after clean up, the amount of tritiated water was measured with liquid scintillation counting to determine the rate of palmitic acid beta-oxidation. PFOS was found to induce fatty acid beta-oxidation at doses starting from a lowest observed effect level (LOEL) of 0.1 ug/g egg weight. Maximum induction of 77% compared to control was seen at 0.3 ug/g. The administered doses in which effects are seen are around and even lower than the levels that can be found in wild populations of birds. General population human levels are a factor of two to three times lower than the LOEL value of this study. The environmental contamination of PFOS therefore presents a possibility of effects in wild populations of birds.

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate/Exposure Summary
text: Palmitic acid's production and use in the manufacture of soaps, lubricating oils, and waterproofing materials and in the synthesis of metal palmitates and food-grade additives will result in its release to the environment through various waste streams. Palmitic acid is a common saturated fatty acid occurring in natural fats and in oils. Fatty acids are an important part of the daily diet of mammals, birds and invertebrates. Palmitic acid is a constituent of various plant parts, tissues, and essential oils of a variety of plant species; it has been identified as a volatile constituent of Korean chamchwi plant and nectarine. If released to air, a vapor pressure of 3.8X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates palmitic acid will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase palmitic acid will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 20 hours. Particulate-phase palmitic acid will be removed from the atmosphere by wet or dry deposition. Palmitic acid does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm and, therefore, is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight. If released to soil, neutral palmitic acid is expected to have no mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 1.3X10+4. The estimated pKa of palmitic acid is 4.95, indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts. Volatilization from moist soil is not expected because the compound exists as an anion and anions do not volatilize. Palmitic acid is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces based upon its vapor pressure. Utilizing a modified OECD screening test accounting for poor water solubility, palmitic acid reached 84% of its theoretical BOD in 28 days, suggesting that biodegradation is expected to be an important environmental fate process under certain environmental conditions in soil. If released into water, neutral palmitic acid is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the estimated Koc. The concentration of palmitic acid decreased from 536 to 3.7 ug/L (half-life approximately 0.50 days) during a 29-day incubation period of freshwater, suggesting that biodegradation may be an important environmental fate process in water under certain conditions. An estimeted pKa of 4.95 indicates palmitic acid will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and, therefore, volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process. An experiemntal BCF of 60 suggests bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is moderate. Hydrolysis is not expected to be an important environmental fate process since this compound lacks functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions (pH 5 to 9). Occupational exposure to palmitic acid may occur through inhalation of powder and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where palmitic acid is produced or used. Monitoring data indicate that the general population may be exposed to palmitic acid via inhalation of ambient air, ingestion of food and drinking water, and dermal contact with consumer products containing palmitic acid. (SRC)

text: Palmitic acid is a saturated fatty acid which occurs in natural fats, oils, and tall oil(1). Palmitic acid occurs as the glyceryl ester in fats and oils(2). Palmitic acid can be obtained from Japan wax or Chinese vegetable tallow(2). Palmitic acid was determined to be a volatile constituent from the Korean chamchwi plant(Aster scaber Thunb)(3). Palmitic acid has been identified as a volatile constituent of nectarine(4). Mature grains of brown rice were found to contain palmitic acid(5). Palmitic acid was found in paprika oleoresin at <0.1 mg/kg(6). This compound is a carboxylic acid that is also known as a fully saturated long chain fatty acid; fatty acids were first isolated by the hydrolysis of naturally occurring fats(7). Fatty acids are widely distributed in nature as components of animal and vegetable fats(8) including lipids such as oils and fats, waxes, sterol esters and other minor compounds(7,8). Palmitic acid is reported found in apple, celery, in the essential oil of lemon and sweet orange, tomato, banana, cranberry, guava, grapes, melon, papaya, pear, raspberry, strawberry, cinnamon, ginger, saffron, hop oil, soybean, avocado, plums, beans, mushroom, starfruit, marjoram, fenugreek, mango, tamarind, fig, kelp, cardamom, rice, prickly pear, dill, licorice, and sweet grass oil(9). Palmitic acid is a constituent of various plant parts, tissues, and essential oils of a variety of plant species(10).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: ATMOSPHERIC FATE: According to a model of gas/particle partitioning of semivolatile organic compounds in the atmosphere(1), palmitic acid, which has a vapor pressure of 3.8X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C(2), will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase palmitic acid is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals(SRC); the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 20 hours(SRC), calculated from its rate constant of 2.0X10-11 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) that was derived using a structure estimation method(3). Particulate-phase palmitic acid may be removed from the air by wet and dry deposition(SRC). Palmitic acid adsorbed on silica gel and irradiated with light at wavelengths greater than 290 nm was found to be 58.9% degraded after 17 hours(4). However, palmitic acid had negligible direct photodegradation in seawater after 5 hours of irradiation under ambient sunlight conditions(5). Palmitic acid does not contain common chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm(6) and, therefore, is not likely susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight under environmental conditions(SRC).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Biodegradation
text: AEROBIC: During a 29-day incubation period of freshwater from the Tama River, Japan, the concentration of palmitic acid decreased from 536 to 3.7 ug/L, suggesting a half-life of approximately 0.50 days(1). Palmitic acid has been listed as an organic chemical easily biodegradable by biological sewage treatment, no data provided(2). Palmitic acid, present at unknown concentrations, reached 2% of its theoretical BOD in 5 days using a sewage inoculum(3). Palmitic acid, present at unknown concentrations, reached 37.2% of its theoretical BOD in 5 days using a sewage inoculum(4). Using the Warburg test method, palmitic acid, present at 500 ppm, reached 2.5% of its theoretical BOD in 1 day using activated sludge solids at a concentration of 2,500 mg/L(5). Using the Warburg test method, the biodegradation of palmitic acid in the presence of an activated sludge inoculum at 25 °C was determined to have a half-life of 3.75 days(6). Palmitic acid, at a concentration of 0.05 ppm in the presence of 50 ug/L activated sludge, produced 37.8% carbon dioxide in 5 days(7). A removal efficiency of 98% was reported for palmitic acid upon analyses of influent and effluent samples collected from the Kallby STP located by the Hoje River, south of Lund, Sweden (8). In a modified OECD screening test accounting for poor water solubility, palmitic acid, present at 20 ppm, reached 84% of its theoretical BOD in 28 days(9).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Biodegradation
text: ANAEROBIC: In the presence of 1-3 g/L total solids of anaerobic digested sludge, palmitic acid in an unknown concn was determined to be 68.7% biodegraded after an incubation period of 60 days; biodegradation was measured as the production of carbon dioxide(1). The anaerobic degradation of 10 mg/L C(14)-labeled palmitic acid in the presence of raw sludge after 28 days yielded 66.1% C(14)-labeled carbon dioxide and 25.6% C(14)-labeled methane(2). The anaerobic degradation of C(14)-labeled palmitic acid in the presence of raw sludge after 28 days gave a first order biodegradation rate as 0.32%/day(3), giving an anaerobic half-life of 52 days(SRC). Freshwater sediment samples taken from Lake Suwa, Japan containing 22.86 mg and 23.66 mg palmitic acid were found to have 38 and 39% methane production after an incubation time of 39 and 48 days, respectively(4).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Abiotic Degradation
text: The rate constant for the vapor-phase reaction of palmitic acid with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals has been estimated as 2.0X10-11 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) using a structure estimation method(1). This corresponds to an atmospheric half-life of about 20 hours at an atmospheric concentration of 5X10+5 hydroxyl radicals per cu cm(1). Palmitic acid is not expected to undergo hydrolysis in the environment due to the lack of functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions(2). Palmitic acid adsorbed on silica gel and irradiated with light at wavelengths greater than 290 nm was found to be 58.9% degraded after 17 hours(3). However, palmitic acid had negligible direct photodegradation in seawater after 5 hours of irradiation under ambient sunlight conditions(4). Palmitic acid does not contain common chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm(2) and, therefore, is not likely susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight under environmental conditions(SRC).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Bioconcentration
text: The bioaccumulation factor of palmitic acid in golden ide fish (Leuciscus idus melanotus), calculated as the concentration of chemical in fish (ug/g) divided by the medium concentration of chemical in water (ug/g), was determined to be 60 after 3 days(1). According to a classification scheme(2), this BCF suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is moderate(SRC). The bioaccumulation factor of palmitic acid in algae (Chlorella fusca), calculated as the concentration of chemical in algae (ug/g) divided by the final concentration of chemical in water (ug/g), was determined to be 8,400 after 1 day(1).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Soil Adsorption/Mobility
text: The Koc of neutral palmitic acid is estimated as 1.3X10+4(SRC), using a log Kow of 7.17(1) and a regression-derived equation(2). According to a classification scheme(3), this estimated Koc value suggests that neutral palmitic acid is expected to be immobile in soil. The estimated pKa of palmitic acid is 4.95(4), indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in the anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts(5).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Volatilization from Water/Soil
text: An estimated pKa of 4.95(1) for palmitic acid indicates this compound will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and therefore volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process(2). Palmitic acid is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces(SRC) based upon a vapor pressure of 3.8X10-7 mm Hg(3).

section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: GROUNDWATER: Groundwater samples taken from wells in the Besos basin, Northeast Spain were found to contain palmitic acid concentrations ranging from 40 to 430 ng/L(1).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: DRINKING WATER: Analysis of a British lowland river, a West German lowland river, and British drinking waters was conducted. Palmitic acid was identified in drinking water, concentrations unknown(1). Palmitic acid was identified in the initial survey of raw and treated water taken at waterworks treating lowland river water in the UK between March and Dec 1976(2). In the survey of treated water, palmitic acid was identified in 5 of 14 samples taken between Feb and June 1979 after new treatment procedures were implemented(2). Palmitic acid was listed as a contaminant found in drinking water for a survey of US cities including Miami, FL, Cincinnati, OH, Ottumwa, IA, New Orleans, LA, Philadelphia, PA, and Seattle, WA(3). Palmitic acid has been identified as an organic disinfection byproduct (DBP) at a pilot plant in Evansville, IN, concentration unknown(4). Tap water from Tsukuba, Japan has been found to contain palmitic acid in unknown concentrations(5). Palmitic acid was identified as an ozone disinfection by-product in drinking water samples from a pilot plant in Jefferson Parish, LA which uses Mississippi River as the raw water source; samples were collected following 4 rounds of ozonation treatment performed in January, 1994, August 1994, May 1995, and September 1996(6).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: SURFACE WATER: Samples of water taken from the Po and Lambro Rivers in Italy, withdrawn from September 1988 to January 1990, were found to contain palmitic acid, concentrations unknown(1). Samples collected from a small segment of the Delaware River just north of Philadelphia in August 1977 were found to contain palmitic acid in concentrations ranging from moderate to very high(2). A total of ten replicate water samples collected at the Inner Harbor Navigation Canal near Lake Pontchartain, New Orleans, LA on June 23, 1980 were found to contain an average of 0.55 ppb palmitic acid from the flood tide and no detection of palmitic acid from the ebb tide(3). Palmitic acid has been identified, not quantified, in a study of 250 samples collected from the Fox River System in Wisconsin from 1976 to 1977(4). Large mass water samples were collected from the Sacramento River, Sacramento County, CA on December 10, 1993, from Putah Creek, Yolo County, CA on November 26, 1993, and from Clear Lake, CA on April 5, 1994; palmitic acid was isolated from the Clear Lake water in unknown concentrations(5).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: RAIN/SNOW/FOG: Eight surface snow samples collected on Antarctic expeditions from 1987/88, 1988/89, and 1990/91 and six deep snow samples collected from the 1990/91 expedition were found to contain an average of 1,630 ng/L palmitic acid in surface Arctic snow(1). Palmitic acid was found at 0.75, 0.52, 1.68, 0.38, 1.25, 0.08, 6.19, and 2.60 ug/kg in snow samples from Nellium, Muonio and Levi, Finland and Butovo, Moscow State University, Shosse Entuziastov and Shuch'e, Russia, and Lake Baikal, Siberia, respectively(2).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Effluent Concentrations
text: An average palmitic acid concentration of 6,500 ng/ul was identified in an industrial wastewater survey in which samples collected between Nov 1, 1979 to Nov 1, 1981 were analyzed(1). Water samples from three secondary treatment publicly owned treatment works in NJ were found to contain average palmitic acid concentrations of 14, 8, and 25 ppb(2). Secondary effluents from ten municipal and industrial wastewater treatment plants discharging into Illinois rivers were sampled; palmitic acid was identified in effluents from St. Charles Public Owned Treatment Work (POTW), Addison POTW, and Bensenville POTW(3). Palmitic acid was found in straw pulp bleaching and combined mill effluents taken during a production week starting on May 20, 1983 in Denmark(4). The average concentration of palmitic acid identified in Los Angeles County effluent collected quarterly from Nov 1980 to Aug 1981 was determined to be 2,500 ug/L(5). Wastewater from two kraft paper mills in Georgia were sampled in March 1972 and found to contain approximately 0.218 and 0.088 mg/L palmitic acid (as the methyl derivative)(6). Palmitic acid has been identified in unknown concentrations of leachate from a sanitary landfill in Barcelona, Spain(7). Palmitic acid has been identified in leachate samples collected from the interior of a municipal landfill situated in Gryta, Vasteras, Sweden in May 1990, concentration unknown(8). Palmitic acid was found in sludges from a Finnish pulp and paper mill(9). Palmitic acid was found in landfill leachate from a municipal solid waste facility in Porto Alegre City, Brazil(10). Palmitic acid was identified in Iona Island Sewage Treatment Plant (British Columbia, Canada) sewage and sludge effluent, concentrations ranging from 229 to 1,345 ug/L(11). Palmitic acid has been identified in sewage treatment effluent water samples from the lower River Lee, North of London, England in large quantities (> 0.1 ug/L)(12). Effluents from two pulp mills located downstream of the Township of Kawerau, in the Eastern Bay of Plenty region, New Zealand were found to contain an average of 311 and 20.5 ppb palmitic acid(13). Palmitic acid was identified in  the emissions of a municipal waste incineration plant in Germany as having a concentration of 36.7 ug/cu m(14). Groundwater and soil from 91 waste sites at 18 Department of Energy (DOE) facilities were analyzed; palmitic acid was found at one of the facilities in groundwater, concentration not quantified(15).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Effluent Concentrations
text: Fine particle aerosol emission rates for palmitic acid from noncatalyst automobiles, catalyst automobiles, and heavy-duty diesel trucks were determined to be 6.0, 63.9, and 153.1 ug/km, respectively(1). Palmitic acid was identified in tire wear particles, brake lining particles, and road dust particles at concentrations of 4,818.4, 83.3, and 1,216.7 ug/g of particle sample, respectively(2). Palmitic acid was found in fine particulate abrasion products from green leaves at a concentration of 835.4 ug/g and from dead leaves at a concentration of 589.9 ug/g; samples collected were from trees characteristic of the Los Angeles, CA area(3). Fine particle emission rates for palmitic acid from a natural gas-fired water heater and a natural gas-fired space heater were determined(4). A HEPA-filtered dilution air sample emission rate for palmitic acid was determined to be 9.7 pg/kJ; the emission rate for palmitic acid through the first filter was determined to be 310.4 pg/kJ; the emission rate for palmitic acid through the backup filter was 56.8 pg/kJ(4). The emission rate for palmitic acid from motor vehicles in the Van Nuys tunnel in Los Angeles at 493.4 mg/L of gasoline-equivalent fuel burned, sampled on Sept 21, 1993(4). name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Sediment/Soil Concentrations
text: SOIL: Palmitic acid was identified 20 meters deep in an effluent irrigated citrus grove in Israel at a concentration of 15 ppb(1). During winter 2002 soil and sand samples, from six locations in the Riyadh metropolitan area of Saudi Arabia, were examined for extractable organic matter; palmitic acid was detected at each location with relative concentrations of 0.06 to 3.25% (of total extractable organic matter)(2).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Atmospheric Concentrations
text: URBAN/SUBURBAN: Sampling of particulate matter and gaseous pollutants was conducted for three weeks between October 7 and 29, 1976 in Belgium; palmitic acid was identified in the gas phase of urban air samples at an average concentration of 4.77 ug/1000 cu m and in particulate samples at an average concentration of 29.03 ug/1000 cu m(1). Palmitic acid was found at 88.4 ng/cu m in samples averaged from central Los Angeles, Azusa and Claremont, CA from samples taken Sept 1993(2). Palmitic acid had an average concentration of 72.6 ng/cu m from 4 urban sites from southern CA from samples taken Sept 8-9, 1993(3). In a study conducted from Sept 14-21, 1982 and Jan 25-31, 1983, air samples taken at three sites along the Niagra River were found to contain palmitic acid(4). Aerosol samples collected in the Tsukuba area northeast of Tokyo, Japan on April 28 and 29, 1985 contained palmitic acid in unknown concentrations(5). Aerosol samples were collected systematically throughout a complete annual cycle (1982) at four urban sites in southern California. Ambient annual concentrations of palmitic acid ranged from 118.3 to 140.5 ng/cu m(6). Palmitic acid was found in Vienna, Austria at 45 ng/cu m from samples taken June 1997(7). A southern CA atmospheric study gave concentrations of 47.4, 63.4, 33.1, 48.7 and 88.5 ng/cu m for Long Beach, Mira Loma, Riverside, San Dimas and Upland, respectively(8). Atmospheric samples taken Dec 26-28, 1995 and Jan 4-6, 1996 in Fresno, CA had palmitic acid in concentrations of 166 and 56.8 ng/cu m and samples taken in Bakersfield had 54.4 and 84.1 ng/cu m, respectively(9). Palmitic acid was found in atmospheric samples from North Birmingham, AL, Jefferson Street, GA, Gulfport, MS, Pensacola, FL and OLF#8, FL (a suburban site 20 km northwest of downtown Pensacola) at concentrations of 19.1, 11.4, 1.79, 8.82 and 1.55 ng/cu m, respectively(10). Palmitic acid was detected at a mean concentration of 310 ng/m cu, with range of 123-424 ng/m cu, in air samples collected between October and December of 2003 at seven locations in Hong Kong(11).

name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Atmospheric Concentrations
text: RURAL/REMOTE: Palmitic acid was found on aerosols obtained over the southern North Atlantic Ocean with a mean concentration of 6.7 ng/cu m and over Chacaltaya, Bolivia with a mean concentration of 3.6 ng/cu-m(1). Palmitic acid was measured in the aerosol form at 170.67, 51.47 and 35.57 ng/cu m at 6am - 12 pm, 12-6 pm and 6 pm-6 am, respectively, in samples taken July 27 to August 8, 1998 in the Pertouli area of the Agrafa Mountains, Greece(2) Analysis of the atmosphere in the Eggegebirge forest in North Rhine-Westflia, western Germany was found to contain palmitic acid, concentrations unknown(3). Palmitic acid was found at 7.8 ng/cu m from Sonnblick Observatory, Austria in samples taken May 1997(4). A southern CA atmospheric study gave palmitic acid concentrations of 8.6, 18.9, 33.1, 5.47, 20.6, 21.6 and 23.3 ng/cu m for Lompoc, Alpine, Atascadero, Lake Arrowhead, Lake Elsinore, Lancaster and Santa Maria, respectively(5). Atmospheric samples taken Dec 26-28, 1995 and Jan 4-6, 1996 in Kern Wildlife Refuge, CA had 9.58 and 10.4 ng/cu m of palmitic acid(6). Palmitic acid concentrations of 7.32, 1.94 and 2.08 ng/cu m were found in Centreville, AL, Yorkville, GA and Oak Grove, MS, respectively(7).

text: Palmitic acid was determined to be a volatile concentrate obtained from the Korean chamchwi plant (Aster scaber Thunb), concentration less than 0.02 % of total sample(1). The fine aerosol emission rate for palmitic acid from a frying hamburger (extra lean/regular), from a charbroiled hamburger (extra lean), and from a charbroiled hamburger (regular) was determined to be 14.2, 83.5, and 481.2 mg/kg, respectively(5). name: Palmitic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Other Environmental Concentrations
text: The environmental impacts of palm oil mill effluent (POME) have been a concern due to the water pollution and greenhouse gases emissions. Thus, this study was conducted to recover the value-added products from POME source before being discharged. The samples, before (X) and after (Y) the pre-recovery system in the clarification tank were sampled and analysed and proximate analysis indicated that both samples are energy rich source of food due to high contents of fats and carbohydrates. GCMS analysis showed that the oil extracts contain predominantly palmitic, oleic, linoleic and stearic acids. Regiospecific analysis of oil extracts by quantitative 13C-NMR spectroscopy demonstrated that both oil extracts contain similar degree of saturation of fatty acids at sn-2 and sn-1,3 positions. The samples are rich in various phytonutrients, pro-vitamin A, vitamin E, squalene and phytosterols, thus contributing to exceptionally high total flavonoid contents and moderate antioxidant activities. Overall, samples X and Y are good alternative food sources, besides reducing the environmental impact of POME.

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Toxicity Summary
text: IDENTIFICATION AND USE: Stearic acid is a solid. It is used in suppositories, coating enteric pills, ointments and for coating bitter remedies. It is also used in manufacturing stearates of aluminum, zinc, and other metals, stearin soap for a liniment invented by Paracelsus, candles, phonograph records, insulators, modeling compounds, impregnating plaster of Paris, in vanishing creams and other cosmetics. Stearic acid is used in animal cell culture. HUMAN STUDIES: The greatest danger from ingestion of large quantities of stearic acid is intestinal obstruction. Skin sensitization is unusual. Aspiration or inhalation of stearic acid could cause chemical pneumonitis. Implantation of stearic acid will cause foreign body reaction. ANIMAL STUDIES: Skin lotion formulations containing 2.8% stearic acid administered at doses of 15 g/kg by gavage to groups of 10 rats resulted in 1 death. Normal behavior and appearance were observed, and there were no gross alterations in surviving rats. No ocular irritation was produced in 6 rabbits by commercial grade stearic acid, whereas mild conjunctival erythema was produced in 3 of 6 rabbits by commercial grade triple-pressed stearic acid. Treatment with 35% stearic acid in corn oil and 50% stearic acid in petrolatum was primarily producing mild conjunctival erythema, which had subsided within 2 days. Intravenous infusion of large doses of stearic acid were thrombogenic in rats, rabbits, and dogs, causing blood platelet aggregation and acute heart failure. When diets containing 5 to 50% stearic acid (as the monoglyceride) were fed to weanling mice for 3 weeks, depression of weight gain was seen above the 10% dietary level. Mortality occurred only with the 50% diet. The effects were less noticeable in adult mice. Rats fed 5% stearic acid as part of a high-fat diet for 6 weeks, or 6% stearic acid for 9 weeks, showed a decreased blood clotting time and hyperlipemia. Rats fed 50 g/kg/day stearic acid for 24 weeks developed reversible lipogranulomas in adipose tissue. No significant pathological lesions were observed in rats fed 3000 ppm stearic acid orally for about 30 weeks, but anorexia, increased mortality, and a greater incidence of pulmonary infection were observed. Single intraperitoneal doses of stearic acid in mice, ranging from approximately 15 to 500 mg/kg, caused no fatalities, but at the highest dose level caused a loss of body weight. In cats, low doses of stearic acid produced elevated pulmonary but decreased systemic blood pressure. Doses greater than 5 mg caused apnea, a fall in blood pressure, and convulsions leading to death. Stearic acid was tested for mutagenicity using the Ames test with Salmonella typhimurium strains TA98, TA100, TA1535, TA1537, and TA1538. Stearic acid had no mutagenic activity over background in the strains tested with and without metabolic activation.

text: Minimal to mild erythema was observed at a few sites after treatment with a lotion formulation containing 2.8% stearic acid or a 1% aqueous dilution of a bar soap formulation containing 23% stearic acid followed by UVA irradiation. text: No reactions were observed in 100 human subjects of a photosensitization study testing an eyeliner formulation containing 2.66% stearic acid. text: Two skin lotion formulations containing 2.8% stearic acid were tested for phototoxicity. Aqueous preparations of the formulations, 100, 75, 50, and 25%, were applied to four different sites on the backs of 10 male Hartley albino guinea pigs weighing 324-486 g and 284-452 g. These sites were exposed to UVA radiation. Ten control guinea pigs weighing 268-434 and 344-464 g received the same topical applications but no UVA irradiation. Sites were evaluated 1 and 24 hr after treatment. Neither formulation was considered phototoxic to the guinea pigs under these conditions because the control group had signs of irritation that were comparable to the irradiated test group. One guinea pig in the control group of one study died. The test groups reactions ranged from questionable to moderate erythema at 6 (50% preparation) to all 10 sites (75%, 100% preparations). The 25% preparations produced no signs of phototoxicity in either study. The control groups in both studies had questionable to moderate (50-100% sites, 50-75% sites) or considerable erythema (100% site). No irritation was observed at control sites treated with the 25% preparations.

section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Non-Human Toxicity Excerpts
text: /LABORATORY ANIMALS: Acute Exposure/ Stearic acid causes hypercoagulability of the blood by activation of factor XII and by aggregation of blood platelets. Injection of unbound stearic acid (sodium salt) into the systemic circulation of dogs was followed by massive generalized thrombosis and sudden death. Similar infusions into birds, which are deficient in factor XII, did not cause hypercoagulability or thrombosis. The effects of the long-chain saturated fatty acids could be prevented by using albumin to bind the stearic acid at a molar ratio of free fatty acid (FFA) to albumin of < 2. The major issue is whether eating foods rich in stearic acid can cause a thrombogenic effect. We have no experimental evidence to support this concept. If a thrombogenic effect of long-chain saturated fatty acids exists in humans, it is most likely to occur as an aberration of fatty acid transport in which the FFA-albumin molar ratio exceeds 2 either as a result of very high plasma FFA concentrations from lipid mobilization or a low concentration of albumin in the blood as found in disease states such as the nephrotic syndrome.

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate/Exposure Summary
text: Stearic acid's production and use in the manufacture of chemicals, especially for stearates and stearate driers, lubricants and soaps, in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics, as an accelerator activator, as a dispersing agent and softener in rubber compounds, in shoe and metal polishes, coatings, food packaging, suppositories and ointments, may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams. Its use as an inert ingredient in pesticides may result in its direct release to the environment. Stearic acid is a fully saturated fatty acid and occurs as a glyceride in tallow and other animal fats and oils, as well as in some vegetable oils. Fatty acids are an important part of the normal daily diet of mammals, birds and invertebrates. Stearic acid is found in low percentages in cotton, coconut, palm kernel, corn, palm, castor, rapeseed, soybean, sunflower, herring, and tallow oils, and in several varieties of rice. If released to air, an estimated vapor pressure of 7.2X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates stearic acid will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase stearic acid will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 17 hours. Particulate-phase stearic acid will be removed from the atmosphere by wet and dry deposition. Stearic acid does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm and, therefore, is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight. If released to soil, stearic acid is expected to have no mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 5.1X10+4. The estimated pKa of stearic acid is 4.75, indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in the anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process because the compound exists as an anion and anions do not volatilize. Stearic acid is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces based upon its estimated vapor pressure. Utilizing a modified OECD screening test stearic acid reached 79% of its theoretical BOD in 28 days, suggesting that biodegradation is an important fate process in soil. If released into water, the neutral species of stearic acid is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the estimated Koc. The stearate, the anion of stearic acid, is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based on experimental studies averaging 99% adsorption. A 5-day theoretical BOD of 43.9% using activated sludge suggests that biodegradation may be an important fate process in water. The estimated pKa indicates stearic acid will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and therefore volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process. An estimated BCF of 10 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. Hydrolysis is not expected to be an important environmental fate process since this compound lacks functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions. Occupational exposure to stearic acid may occur through inhalation of dust and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where stearic acid is produced or used. Monitoring data indicate that the general population may be exposed to stearic acid via inhalation of ambient air and tobacco smoke, ingestion of food and drinking water, and dermal contact with this compound and other consumer products containing stearic acid. (SRC)

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Natural Pollution Sources
text: Stearic acid occurs as a glyceride in tallow and other animal fats and oils, as well as in some vegetable oils(1). Stearic acid is found in low percentages in cotton, coconut, palm kernel, corn, palm, castor, rapeseed, soybean, sunflower, herring, and tallow oils(2). This compound is a carboxylic acid that is also known as a fully saturated long chain fatty acid; fatty acids were first isolated by the hydrolysis of naturally occurring fats(3). Fatty acids are widely distributed in nature as components of animal and vegetable fats(3) including lipids such as oils and fats, waxes, sterol esters and other minor compounds(4).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Artificial Pollution Sources
text: Stearic acid's production and use in the manufacture of chemicals, especially for stearates and stearate driers, lubricants and soaps, in pharmaceuticals and cosmetics, as an accelerator activator, as a dispersing agent and softener in rubber compounds, in shoe and metal polishes, coatings, food packaging, suppositories and ointments(1), may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams. Its use as an inert ingredient in pesticides(2) may result in its direct release to the environment. Stearic acid has been identified as a constituent of tobacco, tobacco smoke, and tobacco smoke substitute(3).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: TERRESTRIAL FATE: Based on a classification scheme(1), an estimated Koc value of 5.1X10+4(SRC), determined from a log Kow of 8.23(2) and a regression-derived equation(3), indicates that the neutral species of stearic acid is expected to be immobile in soil(SRC). The estimated pKa of stearic acid is 4.75(4), indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in the anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts(5). Volatilization from moist soil is not expected because the compound exists as an anion and anions do not volatilize. Stearic acid is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces(SRC) based upon an estimated vapor pressure of 7.22X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C(6). In a modified OECD screening test stearic acid reached 79% of its theoretical BOD in 28 days(7) indicating that biodegradation may be an important fate process in soil(SRC).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: FIELD STUDY: In a 1976 field study using samples from agricultural irrigation water, agricultural runoff, streams, and sewage stabilization ponds collected in Yolo and Sacramento Counties, CA, stearic acid, at a concentration of 0.30 mM, did not produce photooxidants after exposure to 5 hours of sunlight(measured as equivalent hydrogen peroxide levels)(1).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: AQUATIC FATE: Based on a classification scheme(1), an estimated Koc value of 5.1X10+4(SRC), determined from a log Kow of 8.23(2) and a regression-derived equation(3), indicates that neutral species of stearic acid is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment(SRC). The adsorption of stearate, the anion of stearic acid, using relatively nonpolar marine sediment sand surfaces resulted in Kds of 210, 140 and 36, respectively; overall averaging 99% adsorption(4), therefore the stearate is also expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment. An estimated pKa of 4.75(5) indicates stearic acid will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and therefore volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process(6). According to a classification scheme(7), an estimated BCF of 10(SRC), from its log Kow(2) and a regression-derived equation(3), suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low(SRC). During a 29 day incubation period of freshwater from the Tama River, Japan, the concentration of stearic acid decreased from 536 to 3.7 ug/L, suggesting a half-life of approximately 0.50 days(8). A 5 day theoretical BOD of 43.9 % using a marine water inoculum(9) suggests that biodegradation may be an important environmental fate process in water(SRC).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: ATMOSPHERIC FATE: According to a model of gas/particle partitioning of semivolatile organic compounds in the atmosphere(1), stearic acid, which has a vapor pressure of 7.22X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C(2), will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase stearic is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals(SRC); the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 17 hours(SRC), calculated from its rate constant of 2.3X10-11 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) that was derived using a structure estimation method(3). Particulate-phase stearic acid may be removed from the air by wet or dry deposition(SRC). Stearic acid does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm and therefore is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight(3).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Biodegradation
text: AEROBIC: In a modified OECD screening test accounting for poor water solubility, stearic acid, present at 20 ppm, reached 79% of its theoretical BOD in 28 days(1). Stearic acid, present at a concentration range of 2.5 to 20 ppm, reached 44% of its theoretical BOD in 5 days using a sewage inoculum(2). Using the Warburg test method, stearic acid, present at 500 ppm, reached 0.2, 0.6, 1.3% of its theoretical BOD in 0.25, 0.5, and 1 day, respectively, using an activated sludge inoculum with a microbial population of 2,500 mg/L(3). Using the Warburg test method, the biodegradation of stearic acid in the presence of an activated sludge inoculum at 20, 25, and 30 °C was determined to have half-lives of 3.75, 5.55, and 10.7 days, respectively(4). In an aerobic screening test, stearic acid was determined to be 95% degraded in 21 days using a sewage inoculum(5). Using a marine water inoculum, 5 ppm stearic acid was determined to have a theoretical BOD of 43.9% after 5 days(6). In the presence of a sewage inoculum, 39% removal of 0.777 ppm stearic acid occurred at a kraft paper mill lagoon over two days(7). A removal efficiency of 98% was reported for stearic acid upon analyses of influent and effluent samples collected from the Kallby STP located by the Hoje River, south of Lund, Sweden (8).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Biodegradation
text: AEROBIC: The half-lives of stearic acid in Williamsburg surface sandy loam, Williamsburg subsurface silt loam, and Sault Ste Marie subsurface sand were determined to be 1.9, 13, and 3.4 days, respectively(1). Williamsburg silt loam and Sault Ste Marie sand containing 1 ppm stearic acid and dissolved organic carbon of 3,469 and 12,500 ppm total organic carbon were determined to biodegrade fast, with half-lives of 13.025 and 2.9 days, respectively(2). During a 29 day incubation period of freshwater from the Tama River, Japan, the concentration of stearic acid decreased from 536 to 3.7 ug/L, suggesting a half-life of approximately 0.50 days(3).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Biodegradation
text: ANAEROBIC: Freshwater sediment samples taken from Lake Suwa, Japan containing 22.86 mg and 23.66 mg stearic acid were found to have 19 and 25% methane production after an incubation time of 39 and 48 days, respectively(1).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Abiotic Degradation
text: The rate constant for the vapor-phase reaction of stearic acid with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals has been estimated as 2.3X10-11 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) using a structure estimation method(1). This corresponds to an atmospheric half-life of about 14 hours at an atmospheric concentration of 5X10+5 hydroxyl radicals per cu cm(1). Stearic acid is not expected to undergo hydrolysis in the environment due to the lack of functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions(2). Stearic acid does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm(2) and, therefore, is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight(SRC).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Bioconcentration
text: An estimated BCF of 10 was calculated in fish for stearic acid(SRC), using a log Kow of 8.23(1) and a regression-derived equation(2). According to a classification scheme(3), this BCF suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low(SRC).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Soil Adsorption/Mobility
text: The Koc for the neutral species of stearic acid is estimated as 5.1X10+4(SRC), using a log Kow of 8.23(1) and a regression-derived equation(2). According to a classification scheme(3), this estimated Koc value suggests the neutral (non-ionized) species of stearic acid is expected to be immobile in soil. The estimated pKa of stearic acid is 4.75(4), indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in the anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts(5). However, the adsorption of stearate, the anion of stearic acid, was determined using relatively nonpolar marine sediment sand surfaces: in anoxic clastic mud from Cape Lookout Bight, NC (3.5 g/g organic carbon, clay), fine carbonate beach sand from Kahana Stream, Oahu, HI (1.3 g/g organic carbon, fine sand and silty clay), and a fine carbonate sand from Waimanalo Beach, Oahu, HI (0.17 g/g organic carbon, fine-very fine sand), stearate exhibited Kds of 210, 140 and 36, respectively; overall averaging 99% adsorption(6), suggesting that the anionic species will be immobile in soil.

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Volatilization from Water/Soil
text: An estimated pKa of 4.75(1) indicates stearic acid will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and therefore volatilization from water surfaces and moist soil is not expected to be an important fate process(2). Stearic acid is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces(SRC) based upon its vapor pressure of 7.22X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C(3).

section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: GROUNDWATER: Groundwater samples taken from wells in the Besos basin, Northeast Spain were found to contain stearic acid concentrations ranging from 45 to 450 ng/L. Sampling was conducted in May, July November, 1985 and March 1986(1).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: DRINKING WATER: Analysis of British drinking waters was conducted and stearic acid was identified(1). Stearic acid was identified in the initial survey of raw and treated water taken at waterworks treating lowland river water in the UK between March and December 1976(2). In the survey of treated water, stearic acid was identified in 3 of 14 samples taken between Feb and June 1979 after new treatment procedures were implemented(2). Stearic acid has been identified in drinking water, concentrations unknown(3). Stearic acid was listed as a contaminant found in drinking water for a survey of US cities including Miami, FL, Cincinnati, OH, Ottumwa, IA, and Seattle, WA(4). Stearic acid has been identified in both raw water and treated water samples after several disinfection process at a pilot plant in Evansville, IN(5). Tap water from Tsukuba, Japan has been found to contain stearic acid(6). Stearic acid was identified as an ozone disinfection by-product in drinking water samples from a pilot plant in Jefferson Parish, LA which uses Mississippi River was as the raw water source; samples were collected following 4 rounds of ozonation treatment performed in January, 1994, August 1994, May 1995, and September 1996(7).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: SURFACE WATER: Stearic acid was identified in samples of water taken from the Po and Lambro Rivers in Italy, Sept 1988 to Jan 1990(1). Water samples collected in England from the River Irwell, River Etherow, and River Mersey in 1984 had average stearic acid concentrations of 12.55, 3.05, and 2.10 ug/L, respectively(2). Samples from the Delaware River north of Philadelphia, PA in Aug 1977 had stearic acid concentrations ranging from moderate to very high(3). Ten replicate water samples collected at the Inner Harbor Navigation Canal near Lake Pontchartain, New Orleans, LA on June 23, 1980 contained an average of 0.6 ppb stearic acid from the flood tide and was not detected from the ebb tide(4). Stearic acid has been identified, not quantified, in a study of 250 samples collected from the Fox River System in Wisconsin from 1976 to 1977(5). Large mass water samples were collected from the Sacramento River, Sacramento County, CA on Dec 10, 1993, from Putah Creek, Yolo County, CA on Nov 26, 1993, and from Clear Lake, CA on April 5, 1994; stearic acid was detected in Clear Lake water at unknown concentrations(6). Stearic acid was not detected in a British lowland river and a West German lowland river(7).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: RAIN/SNOW/FOG: Eight surface snow samples collected on Antarctic expeditions from 1987/88, 1988/89, and 1990/91 and six deep snow samples collected from the 1990/91 expedition were found to contain an average of 534.25 ng/L stearic acid in surface Arctic snow and an average of 32 ng/L stearic acid (as the methyl ester) in deep snow(1). Stearic acid was found at 1.14, 0.20, 0.20, 0.67, 0.14, 0.37 and 1.43 ug/kg in snow samples from Neulaniemi, Nellium, Muonio and Levi, Finland and Butovo, Moscow State University and Shuch'e, Russia, respectively(2).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Effluent Concentrations
text: An average stearic acid concentration of 355 ng/uL was identified in an industrial wastewater survey in which samples collected between Nov 1, 1979 to Nov 1, 1981 were analyzed(1). Water samples from three secondary treatment publicly owned treatment works in NJ were found to contain average stearic acid concentrations of 9.5, 1.2, and 12 ppb(2). Secondary effluents from ten municipal and industrial wastewater treatment plants discharging into Illinois rivers were sampled; stearic acid was identified in effluents from one site (Addison Public Owned Treatment Works)(3). Stearic acid was found in straw pulp bleaching and combined mill effluents taken during a production week starting on May 20, 1983 in Denmark(4). The average concentration of stearic acid identified in Los Angeles County, CA effluent collected quarterly from November 1980 to August 1981 was determined to be 1,000 ug/L(5). Stearic acid was found in trace amounts from municipal landfill leachates in Gryta, Sweden(6). Wastewater from two kraft paper mills in GA sampled in March 1972 contained approximately 0.061 and 0.073 mg/l stearic acid (as the methyl derivative)(7). Water samples taken from the effluent of a kraft paper mill located on the shore of Lake Saimaa, Lappeenranta, Finland was found to contain a stearic acid concentration ranging from 5 to 480 ug/L over a 9 day period(8). Stearic acid was identified in Iona Island Sewage Treatment Plant(British Columbia, Canada) sewage and sludge effluent, concentrations ranging from 240 to 728 ug/L(9). Stearic acid, as the methyl derivative, has been identified in sewage treatment effluent water samples from the lower River Lee, North of London, England in large quantities (> 0.1 ug/L)(10). Effluents from two pulp mills located downstream of the Township of Kawerau, in the Eastern Bay of Plenty region, New Zealand were found to contain average concentrations of 196 and 8.5 ppb stearic acid(11). Samples collected from the Prestwich Sewage Treatment Plant effluent in 1984 had average stearic acid concentrations of 8.65 ug/L(12). Stearic acid has been identified in leachate samples collected from the interior of a municipal landfill situated in Gryta, Vasteras, Sweden in May 1990(13). Stearic acid has been identified in the influent (41.00 ug/L) and effluent (0.80 ug/L) from the Kallby STP located by the Hoje River, south of Lund, Sweden (14).

name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Effluent Concentrations
text: Stearic acid was identified, concentration unknown, as a component of influent and effluent gas samples taken from refuse waste in Singapore(1). Stearic acid was found in candle smoke from paraffin and beeswax at 10.66 and 1.85 mg/g of organic compounds(2). Stearic acid was found in wood smoke from red maple(3), red oak(3), white birch(3), white pine(3), hemlock(3), balsam fir(3), yellow poplar(4), white ash(4), sweet gum(4), mockernut hickory(4), loblolly pine(4), and slash pine(4). name: Stearic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Effluent Concentrations
text: Fine particle aerosol emission rates for stearic acid from noncatalyst automobiles, catalyst automobiles, and heavy-duty diesel trucks were determined to be 3.0, 18.0, and 72.5 ug/km, respectively(1). Fine particle emission rates for stearic acid from a natural gas-fired water heater and a natural gas-fired space heater were determined(5). A HEPA-filtered dilution air sample emission rate for stearic acid was determined to be 2.6 pg/kJ; the emission rate for stearic acid through the first filter was determined to be 81.8 pg/kJ; the emission rate for stearic acid through the backup filter was not determined(5). section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Atmospheric Concentrations
text: URBAN/SUBURBAN: Sampling of particulate matter and gaseous pollutants was conducted for three weeks between October 7 and 29, 1976 in Belgium; stearic acid was identified in the gas phase of urban air samples with an average concentration of 2.27 ug/1000 cu m and in particulate samples with an average concentration of 35.70 ug/1000 cu m(1). section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Antidote and Emergency Treatment
text: /SRP:/ Immediate first aid: Ensure that adequate decontamination has been carried out. If patient is not breathing, start artificial respiration, preferably with a demand-valve resuscitator, bag-valve-mask device, or pocket mask, as trained. Perform CPR as necessary. Immediately flush contaminated eyes with gently flowing water. Do not induce vomiting. If vomiting occurs, lean patient forward or place on left side (head-down position, if possible) to maintain an open airway and prevent aspiration. Keep patient quiet and maintain normal body temperature. Obtain medical attention. /Organic acids and related compounds/

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Antidote and Emergency Treatment
text: /SRP:/ Basic treatment: Establish a patent airway (oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway, if needed). Suction if necessary. Watch for signs of respiratory insufficiency and assist respirations if necessary. Administer oxygen by nonrebreather mask at 10 to 15 L/min. Monitor for pulmonary edema and treat if necessary ... . Monitor for shock and treat if necessary ... . For eye contamination, flush eyes immediately with water. Irrigate each eye continuously with 0.9% saline (NS) during transport ... . Do not use emetics. For ingestion, rinse mouth and administer 5 mL/kg up to 200 mL of water for dilution if the patient can swallow, has a strong gag reflex, and does not drool. Activated charcoal is not effective ... . Do not attempt to neutralize because of exothermic reaction. Cover skin burns with dry, sterile dressings after decontamination ... . /Organic acids and related compounds/

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Antidote and Emergency Treatment
text: /SRP:/ Advanced treatment: Consider orotracheal or nasotracheal intubation for airway control in the patient who is unconscious, has severe pulmonary edema, or is in severe respiratory distress. Early intubation, at the first sign of upper airway obstruction, may be necessary. Positive-pressure ventilation techniques with a bag valve mask device may be beneficial. Consider drug therapy for pulmonary edema ... . Consider administering a beta agonist such as albuterol for severe bronchospasm ... . Monitor cardiac rhythm and treat arrhythmias as necessary ... . Start IV administration of D5W /SRP: "To keep open", minimal flow rate/. Use 0.9% saline (NS) or lactated Ringer's (LR) if signs of hypovolemia are present. For hypotension with signs of hypovolemia, administer fluid cautiously. Consider vasopressors if patient is hypotensive with a normal fluid volume. Watch for signs of fluid overload ... . Use proparacaine hydrochloride to assist eye irrigation ... . /Organic acids and related compounds/

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Human Toxicity Excerpts
text: /HUMAN EXPOSURE STUDIES/ Several bar soap formulations with concentrations of oleic acid ranging from 2.53 to 92.7% were tested for skin irritation using 16 human subjects. A 0.2 mL volume of 8% aqueous preparations was applied to the ventral skin of the forearm under occlusive patches once daily for 5 days using the Frosch and Kligman soap chamber test. The formulations were considered "slightly" to "moderately irritating." The erythema scores ranged from 1.41 to 3.21 on a scale of 0 to 5 and were not directly related to oleic acid concentrations in the formulations.

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Human Toxicity Excerpts
text: /HUMAN EXPOSURE STUDIES/ In a cumulative irritation study, approximately 9.3 mL of each of 2 mascara formulations, a black cream and a brown cream, containing 6% oleic acid were applied to the backs of 14 female and 1 male panelist using closed patches. The panelists removed the patches after 23 hr and bathed. Reactions were scored 24 hr after sample application. The samples were reapplied daily to the same test sites for 21 consecutive days or until irritation scores of 3, corresponding to erythema and papules, were observed. Up to 7 panelists had minimum scores of 1 or slight erythema by the 5th application, and 3 to 4 panelists had maximal scores of 3 and 4 for erythema, papules, or edema by the 14th application. The total irritation scores for the formulations, a summation of the scores over the number of applications and panelists, were 212 and 204 compared with a maximal score of 945. Mean scores were 14.1 and 13.6 compared with a maximal score of 63. The positive control, an aerosol deodorant concentrate, had a total score of 828 and mean score of 55.2. The negative control, a clear liquid baby oil formulation, had a total score of 18 and a mean score of 1.2. The formulations were considered "slightly irritating".

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Human Toxicity Excerpts
text: /HUMAN EXPOSURE STUDIES/ The maximization test was used to test a black cream mascara formulation containing 6% oleic acid for contact sensitization. Induction sites on the volar aspect of the 14 subjects' forearms were pre-treated with single 24-hr occlusive patches of 5% aqueous sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS). Five alternate-day 48-hr occlusive induction patches were followed by a 10-14-day nontreatment period. After pretreatment of new sites with single 30-min occlusive patches of 2% aqueous SLS, single 48-hr occlusive challenge patches were applied. Results for the sites treated with the formulation were similar to those for control sites treated with petrolatum alone and petrolatum plus SLS, respectively. There was "no significant irritation or evidence of contact sensitization".

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Toxicological Information > Human Toxicity Excerpts
text: /HUMAN EXPOSURE STUDIES/ In a repeated insult patch test (RIPT), 200 human volunteers were tested for contact sensitization of a purple wax cosmetic formulation containing 5.0% oleic acid. Nine 24-hr closed induction patches containing 0.3 mL of the formulation were applied to sites on the volar forearm on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays of 3 consecutive weeks during the induction phase of the study. Signs of irritation were scored 48 or 72 hr after the application. After a 10-14 day nontreatment period, a single 48-hr challenge patch was made to a separate site, and the site was scored 48-hr and 72-hr to 96-hr after application. Of the 200 subjects, 153 completed the study. Slight irritation was observed in 1 to 3 subjects during the induction phase, and 1 subject reacted slightly to the challenge patch after 48 hr. "No contact sensitization" was produced by the formulation under the conditions of this study.

text: /LABORATORY ANIMALS: Acute Exposure/ Marked irritation characterized by crusting, ulceration, and thickening of the skin was observed following topical application of commercial grade oleic acid to the skin of rabbits, guinea pigs, and mice. Microscopically, hyperkeratosis, pronounced acanthosis, follicular keratotic plugs, hyperplasia of sebaceous glands, and loss of hair shafts from follicles were observed. Treated skin returned to normal when treatment was discontinued.

text: /AQUATIC SPECIES/ The toxicities of chemicals found in bleached kraft pulp mill effluent were assessed using a sea urchin sperm toxicity test. Sperm of the purple sea urchin, Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, were preincubated with 12 individual compounds, including resin acids, unsaturated fatty acids, their chlorinated derivatives and chlorinated guaiacols. Sperm were then coincubated with eggs and inhibition of fertilization and the effects on sperm motility were assessed. Resin acids, which are highly toxic to juvenile salmonids in freshwater, were less toxic in seawater (EC50s ranging from 2 to more than 20 mg/L). Unsaturated linoleic and linolenic fatty acids inhibited fertilization at lower concentrations (EC50s of 0.28 to 1.07 mg/L) than resin acids, although they are less toxic than resin acids to freshwater fishes. Oleic acid was not significantly toxic up to 75 mg/L. Chlorinated derivatives showed increasing toxicity with increasing chlorination, and chlorinated resin acids were more toxic than their unchlorinated parent compound. Dichlorostearic acid was the most toxic compound tested, with an EC50 of 0.057 mg/L. All compounds except fatty acids inhibited sperm motility.  These results indicate that some of the major constituents of pulp mill effluent exhibit very different levels of toxicity in seawater using a sea urchin sperm cell toxicity test as compared to freshwater bioassays using juvenile salmonids. In addition, mechanisms of action on the sperm appear to differ among the compounds. Accurate quantification of the compounds in effluent as well as the potential effect of the effluent on other marine organisms remains to be determined.

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate/Exposure Summary
text: Oleic acid's production and use in soft soap and other oleates, in polishing compounds, waterproofing textiles, oiling wool, lubricating oils, ointments, cosmetics, ore flotation, surface coatings, and food grade additives may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams. Oleic acid, a fatty acid, occurs as a natural product in the essential oils of various plants and animals. Fatty acids are an important part of the normal daily diet of mammals, birds and invertebrates. If released to air, a vapor pressure of 5.46X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates oleic acid will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase oleic acid will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-lives for this reaction in air is estimated to be 5.1 and 4.6 hours for the cis- and trans- isomers, respectively. Vapor-phase oleic acid will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with ozone; half-lives of about 2.1 and 1.4 hours for the cis- and trans- isomers, respectively, are calculated for this reaction. Particulate-phase oleic acid will be removed from the atmosphere by wet or dry deposition. Oleic acid does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm and therefore is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight. If released to soil, undissociated oleic acid is expected to have no mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 340,000. The pKa of oleic acid is 5.02, indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts. Biodegradation is expected to be an important fate process in soil based on half-lives of 0.2 and 0.66 days in screening tests. If released into water, undissociated oleic acid is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the estimated Koc. Oleic acid was biodegraded 25-30% in the water column in field studies. Based upon the pKa oleic acid will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and therefore volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process. An estimated BCF of 10 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. Hydrolysis is not expected to be an important environmental fate process since this compound lacks functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions. Occupational exposure to oleic acid may occur through dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where oleic acid is produced or used. Monitoring data indicate that the general population may be exposed to oleic via inhalation of ambient air, ingestion of food and drinking water, and dermal contact with this compound and other products containing oleic acid. (SRC)

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: TERRESTRIAL FATE: Based on a classification scheme(1), an estimated Koc value of 340,000 for the free acid(SRC), determined from a log Kow of 7.64(2) and a regression-derived equation(3), indicates that undissociated oleic acid is expected to be immobile in soil(SRC). The pKa of oleic acid is 5.02(4), indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts(5). Volatilization of oleic acid from moist soil is not expected to be an important fate process because the acid is in the anion form and anions do not volatilize(SRC). Oleic acid is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces(SRC) based upon a vapor pressure of 5.46X10-7 mm Hg(6). Biodegradation is expected to be an important fate process in soil based on half-lives of 0.2 and 0.66 days in screening tests(7,8).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: AQUATIC FATE: Based on a classification scheme(1), an estimated Koc value of 340,000 for the free acid(SRC), determined from a log Kow of 7.64(2) and a regression-derived equation(3), indicates that undissociated oleic acid is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment(SRC). A pKa of 5.02(4) indicates oleic acid will exist almost entirely in the anion form at pH values of 5 to 9 and therefore volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process(5). According to a classification scheme(6), an estimated BCF of 10(SRC), from its log Kow(2) and a regression-derived equation(7), suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low(SRC). A 47 and 52 theoretical %BOD for oleic acid measured over a period of 5 days using sewage inoculum(8) and a biodegradation half-life of 0.66 days using activated sludge inocula(9) suggest that biodegradation may be an important environmental fate process in aquatic ecosystems(SRC).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Fate
text: ATMOSPHERIC FATE: According to a model of gas/particle partitioning of semivolatile organic compounds in the atmosphere(1), oleic acid, which has a vapor pressure of 5.46X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C(2), will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase oleic acid is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals(SRC); the half-life for cis-oleic acid and trans-oleic acid reactions in air are estimated to be 5.1 and 4.6 hours(SRC), calculated from rate constants of 7.6X10-11 and 8.3X10-11cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) that were derived using a structure estimation method(3). Vapor-phase oleic acid is also degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with ozone(SRC); the half-life for cis-oleic acid and trans-oleic acid reactions in air are estimated to be 2.1 and 1.4 hours(SRC), respectively, calculated from rate constants of 1.3X10-16 and 2.0X10-16 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) that were derived using a structure estimation method(3). Particulate-phase oleic acid may be removed from the air by wet or dry deposition(SRC). Oleic acid does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm and therefore is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight(4).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Biodegradation
text: AEROBIC: A 47 and 52 theoretical %BOD for oleic acid (initial concn of 1,000 ppm) was measured over a period of 5 days in screening tests at 20 °C using sewage inoculum(1). A biodegradation half-life of 0.66 days was measured for oleic acid at an initial concn of 100 ppm with an aerobic Warburg respirometer at 25 °C using activated sludge inocula(2). In another screening study a first order rate constant was measured to be 0.12/hr for oleic acid (initial concn of 100 ppm) which corresponds to a biodegradation half-life of 0.2 days(3). Oleic acid at initial concns of 1, 10, 1, and 10 ppm exhibited 90, 24, 97, and 28 theoretical %BOD, respectively, over incubation periods of 5, 5, 10, and 10 days, respectively, in an aerobic screening study using sewage inoculum(4). A 68 theoretical %BOD (initial concn of 100 ppm) was measured over a period of 5 days in a screening test at 20 °C using sewage inoculum(5). A 39 theoretical %BOD for oleic acid (initial concn not given) was measured over a period of 5 days in a screening test at 20 °C using sewage inoculum(6). After a 16 day acclimation time, a 63.5 theoretical %BOD was measured for oleic acid (initial concn not given) over a period of 5 days in a screening test at 20 °C using activated sludge inocula(7). A 57.2 theoretical %BOD was measured for oleic acid (initial concn of 500 ppm) over a period of 5 days in an aerobic screening test at 20 °C using activated sludge inoculum(8).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Biodegradation
text: In a field study at Brunswick, GA paper mill in an aerated stabilization basin oleic acid was biodegraded 23-40% and 6-32% in aerated tests run Sept 1995 and May 1996, respectively(1). Oleic acid was biodegraded 10-30% and 1-26% in nonaerated studies also run in the stabilization basin(1). Oleic acid was biodegraded 25-30% in the water column of Leaf river system in New Augusta, MS in activated sludge treatment field tests run Sept 1995(1).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Abiotic Degradation
text: The rate constant for the vapor-phase reaction of cis- and trans-oleic acid with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals have been estimated as 7.6X10-11 and 8.3X10-11 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC), respectively, using a structure estimation method(1). This corresponds to atmospheric half-lives of about 5.1 and 4.6 hours at an atmospheric concentration of 5X10+5 hydroxyl radicals per cu cm(1). The rate constant for the vapor-phase reaction of cis- and trans-oleic acid with ozone has been estimated as 1.3X10-16 and 2.0X10-16 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC), respectively, derived using a structure estimation method(1). This corresponds to atmospheric half-lives of about 2.1 and 1.4 hours at an atmospheric concentration of 7X10+11 ozone molecules per cu cm(2). Oleic acid is not expected to undergo hydrolysis in the environment due to the lack of functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions(3). Oleic acid does not contain chromophores that absorb at wavelengths >290 nm and therefore is not expected to be susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight(3).

text: DRINKING WATER: Oleic acid was qualitatively detected in drinking water concentrate from New Orleans, LA on January 14, 1976, Cincinnati, OH on January 14, 1980, and Seattle, WA on November 5, 1976(1). Oleic acid was qualitatively identified in water from a British drinking water supply(2).

section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: SURFACE WATER: Oleic acid was detected not quantified in the lower Fox River, Wisconsin(1). During summer and fall of 1990, oleic acid was detected at a maximum concn of 12 ug/L from 13 water samples taken in northern Alberta, Canada(3).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Environmental Water Concentrations
text: RAIN/SNOW/FOG: Oleic acid was found at 0.22, 0.10, 0.14, 0.47 and 2.11 ug/kg in snow samples from Nellium and Muonio, Finland and Butovo, Moscow State University and Shosse Entuziastov, Russia, respectively(1).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Effluent Concentrations
text: Wastewater from olive oil production contains oleic acid(1). Oleic acid was qualitatively identified in advanced waste treatment concentrates from Orange County on January 27, 1976 and February 3, 1976 and from Blue Plains, Washington DC(2). Frying of extra-lean and regular hamburger was found to emit 10.1 mg oleic acid/kg meat(3). Charbroiling of extra-lean and regular hamburger was found to emit 82.4-568 mg oleic acid/kg meat(3); it was suggested that meat cooking operations may be an important source of organic aerosol emissions in Los Angeles, CA(3). Oleic acid is present in kraft paper mill wastewaters(4). Oleic acid was found at a concn of 60-891 ug/L in wastewater at the Iona treatment plant in Vancouver, British Columbia(5). Oleic acid was qualitatively identified in wheat and rye straw pulp mill effluents(6). Oleic acid was detected at a concn range of 6-11 ppb in publically owned treatment work effluents from three New Jersey facilities(7). cis-Oleic acid was found at 333.8 ug/g from heated roofing tar pot fumes(8).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Effluent Concentrations
text: Both the cis- and trans- isomers of oleic acid were found in wood smoke from red maple(1), red oak(1), white pine(1), hemlock(1), balsam fir(1), yellow poplar(2), white ash(2), sweet gum(2), mockernut hickory(2), loblolly pine(2), and slash pine(2). trans-Oleic acid was found in wood smoke from paper birch(1). cis-Oleic acid was detected in wood smoke from pine, oak and synthetic logs at 7.62, 1.15 and 0.93 mg/kg of wood burnt(3).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Sediment/Soil Concentrations
text: SEDIMENT: During summer and fall of 1990, oleic acid was detected at a maximum concn of 4.3 ug/g from 21 sediment samples taken in northern Alberta(1). Oleic acid was detected in sediment from lake Jusan and Mutsu Bay, in Japan(2). Oleic acid was detected in sediment in 4 of 7 sites in the German Bight area(3).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Atmospheric Concentrations
text: URBAN/SUBURBAN: Oleic acid was qualitatively detected in airborne particulate matter in a suburban area in Japan(1). Oleic acid was qualitatively found in the gas phase in air from an unknown urban area and it was quantitatively identified in particulate samples at concns of 1.31-2.68 ug/1000 cu m(2). Oleic acid had an average concentration of 7.7 ng/cu m in 4 urban sites from southern CA from samples taken Sept 8-9, 1993(3).

name: Oleic acid
section: Toxicity > Ecological Information > Atmospheric Concentrations
text: RURAL/REMOTE: Oleic acid was found at concns of 190 ng/cu m in January of 1981, 3.6 ng/cu m in July of 1981, and 2.1 ng/cu m in August of 1981 from aerosol samples taken 1 m above ground level in a heavily vegetated area of American Samoa(1). Oleic acid was detected at a concn of 0.043 ng/cu m in an aerosol sample taken above the North Pacific Ocean During May, 1986(1). The mean concn of oleic acid in aerosols over the North Atlantic Ocean was 1.6 ng/cu m in 1978(2). Oleic acid was measured in the gas form at 24.5, 5.76 and 7.33 ng/cu m and in the aerosol form at 16.9, 7.23, and 12.37 ng/cu m at 6AM to 12PM, 12PM to 6PM, and 6PM to 6AM, respectively, in samples taken July 27 to August 8, 1998 in the Pertouli area of the Agrafa Mountains, Greece(3).
